title: The petition
hookLine: here the one praying says why this Ardas is being made

cards: Sunday at the gurdwara. The congregation stands, hands joined, and the person leading the Ardas has been speaking for several minutes: the Gurus, the martyrs, the Khalsa, the gurdwaras far away, the honor of the humble.
Then the voice changes slightly. A name is spoken, a family's name, perhaps. A new baby.
A grandfather's surgery next week. A shop opening on Main Street. A student leaving for college.
For a few seconds, a prayer that belongs to a whole people becomes about one household's Tuesday.

teach.b: This is the petition, the part of the Ardas where the reason is named.
Everything before it is fixed and shared: the opening invokes the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib, then come the remembrances, the requests for the Khalsa and for the Sikhs, the line about maan.
Then the one leading says something like: in Your presence, this Ardas is made for, and the reason is named in plain words. The congregation listens and joins the waheguru that follows.

teach.h: ARDAS: A PETITION TO A COURT.
teach.b: Some readers trace the word ardas to a Persian word for a written petition, the kind a person would hand up to a ruler's court. Whatever the root, the picture fits. A petition isn't a speech.
It's short, it's specific, and it names what is being asked. And notice who can be named. Not only the person leading.

A family can ask the granthi to include their purpose: thanks for a safe journey, a new job, the anniversary of a death, a child's exam. At home, a person praying alone names their own reason the same way.
Nothing in the prayer asks for the reason to be grand, only plain. There's something steadying in that.
The big, shared prayer holds a whole people's history, and inside it, your small reason is given a place, said out loud, in front of the Guru. Nobody is too small to have their reason named.
And the prayer doesn't stop at one household: before it ends, it turns back out toward everyone.

how: In the gurdwara, a family can ask the granthi to name their purpose in the Ardas, a birth, a journey, a remembrance; at home, the person praying names their own reason at the same point.

games.q: your grandfather has surgery next week. you're at the gurdwara for the Sunday Ardas. what can you do?
o: ask the granthi to name his surgery in the Ardas.
games.why: families often ask for their purpose to be named. the shared prayer makes room for one household's need.

practice: Let today's real concern rise, not the one you think you should have, but the one that's actually there: a worry, a hope, a thank-you.

Put it into one plain sentence, no flourishes: this is for my mother's appointment, or, this is thanks for the week. If you pray, say that sentence quietly to the One; if not, just let it sit in the open.

wordCard.voice: The petition. The moment in the Ardas when the reason for this prayer is named in plain words, inside a prayer that belongs to everyone.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the standing prayer; some readers trace it to Persian arz-dasht, a written petition.

carryVoice: Your line: say why. A short, honest reason, said in front of the Guru. Day six hundred thirty-three, done.
